The Green manakin (Cryptopipo holochlora) is a small passerine endemic to the lowland rainforests of Central and South America. Field studies examining the species' basal metabolic rate have documented a maximum oxygen consumption of 38.18 milliliters per hour [JOi = 38.18 milliliters per hour] when individuals are resting under stable thermal conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This comparatively elevated metabolic performance, approaching levels seen in manakins of similar body size, likely reflects the high energetic demands of the species' lekking behavior and its frugivorous diet. The female members of this species reach an ultimate wet body mass of 14.9 grams [Wwi = 14.9 grams] as adults, a figure that corresponds to values predicted by allometric equations for neotropical passerines. Hatchlings emerge from eggs that measure 20 millimeters in length and 15 millimeters in width, proportions that yield a calculated initial wet weight of 2.36 grams [Ww0 = 2.36 grams] based on the standard formula for an ellipsoid egg.

Incubation biology in Cryptopipo holochlora reveals a tightly constrained developmental schedule. Eggs incubated at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] require a period of 12 days [ab = 12 days] to complete embryonic development and produce a hatchling. This relatively brief incubation interval, typical of many small-bodied tyrannoid passerines, reflects the altricial state of the neonate at emergence. The transition from a hatchling mass of 2.36 grams [Ww0 = 2.36 grams] to the adult female asymptotic mass of 14.9 grams [Wwi = 14.9 grams] represents a greater than sixfold increase in body mass, a trajectory that demands sustained parental provisioning throughout the nestling period. Observations of captive pairs suggest that egg dimensions are remarkably consistent, with clutches invariably containing eggs whose length and width conform to the species-specific mean of 20 millimeters in length and 15 millimeters in width. The correlation between egg size and hatchling mass is particularly strong in this species, underscoring the importance of yolk reserves for the early developmental stages.

Under the ambient thermal regime typical of the species' active metabolic phase, which centers on 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the fledgling achieves its first flight at 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching]. This rapid achievement of flight capacity is an adaptive response to the elevated predation risk that characterizes the understory where manakin nests are concealed. In contrast to the pace of fledging, the onset of reproductive maturity follows a considerably more protracted schedule; puberty is attained at 39 days after hatching [tp = 39 days after hatching] under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This temporal separation between fledging and maturation allows the juvenile ample time to refine foraging skills and establish the spatial familiarity required for successful territory defense. The species' maximum lifespan, documented from marked individuals in long-term study plots, extends to 10 years [am = 10 years] when maintained at 40.2 °C, a longevity that places it among the longer-lived members of the Pipridae family at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Reproductive output in the Green manakin is characterized by a modest annual investment. Females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], with roughly one clutch per year [F_R_i = roughly one clutch per year] representing the typical frequency in undisturbed populations. This low fecundity is consistent with the life-history strategy of a species that invests heavily in each offspring over a prolonged period of parental care. The age at which a female first successfully produces a brood has been recorded at 401.5 days after hatching [tR = 401.5 days after hatching] under laboratory conditions maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay between the attainment of puberty at 39 days after hatching [tp = 39 days after hatching] and the first reproductive event at 401.5 days after hatching [tR = 401.5 days after hatching] reflects the considerable time required for a young female to acquire a territory, establish a social position within the lek, and accumulate sufficient body condition to support egg production at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Comparative analysis of life-history traits across manakin species reveals that Cryptopipo holochlora occupies an intermediate position on the slow-fast continuum. The species achieves a maximum documented lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] under optimal thermal conditions, which is comparable to that of other Pipridae of equivalent body size at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Its reproductive strategy of producing a single egg per clutch and a single clutch per year reflects an investment in offspring quality over quantity. The asymptotic adult mass of 14.9 grams [Wwi = 14.9 grams] in females is typical for a frugivore of this size, while the initial hatchling mass of 2.36 grams [Ww0 = 2.36 grams] is relatively high, approximately 16 percent of maternal mass, underscoring the large relative egg size characteristic of the genus. Further physiological studies could usefully examine how metabolic rate scales with body temperature in the field.
